description:
Grupo de nerds de La Plata y Tandil.

El nombre de nuestro equipo es en honor al CubeSat Atenea, desarrollado en nuestro país y desplegado recientemente por la misión Artemis en su camino a la Luna.
summary:
In this project, we created a virtual museum powered by official resources from the NASA to deliver an immersive online experience. Our goal is to give people of all ages, anywhere in the world, the chance to explore the probes, landers, and rovers that made our current knowledge of the solar system possible. Using NASA’s 3D models, official image galleries, e-books, and mission archives, we brought the history of Moon and Mars (and, more broadly, Solar System) exploration together in one place. The platform also features a timeline of major aerospace milestones and a dedicated deep space section. 
NASA provides information on its website about the abandoned (but not forgotten) artifacts that served this goal, but in a format that is not necessarily accessible or engaging for the general public. We aim to encourage new generations to get into science, engage in space exploration, and value the knowledge that all of these missions provided. 
We view this prototype as the foundation for a much fuller version in the future, and we hope people enjoy exploring it.
details:
Our project is structured as an interactive digital museum. A museum is an institution devoted to preserving and exhibiting humanity’s historical and cultural heritage. The history of space exploration is part of such heritage. However, many of the artifacts that played a central role in that history are located far away from home, on the surfaces of or in orbit around other celestial bodies. Bringing them back to Earth to exhibit them and showcase their contributions to scientific knowledge is impossible. Therefore, we believe that a digital museum is a suitable way to provide the public with information about these artifacts.

To present this information, we used a storytelling approach aimed at establishing an emotional connection between users and the artifacts whose stories are being told. Beyond providing information, these stories seek to convey a message by highlighting not only the protagonists’ achievements, but also the challenges they might have encountered along the way, and how they overcame them. To foster the empathy that storytelling seeks to evoke, each story is narrated in the first person by its protagonist. Animations, simulated conversations with users, interactive games, and other resources are combined to create an engaging experience. 

The project’s website features different tabs representing the museum’s wings, allowing users to easily select which stories they would like to explore. The Moon and Mars tabs also present a map of these celestial bodies’ surfaces, showing the location of the artefacts whose stories are featured on the webpage. The Deep Space tab includes a NASA resource that allows users to visualize, in real time, the locations of probes that are still traveling through space in real-time. Additionally, the museum includes a timeline, containing key information about the artifacts.

What age group is your story designed for?

The museum is designed for a general public of all ages. Rather than targeting experts, it aims to engage people who are curious about space exploration by presenting information in an accessible and enjoyable way.

How accessible is the format you chose to use?

The format is accessible considering that any person with internet connection can enjoy the experience on any device. Although the prototype does not yet conform to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), implementing these standards requires more time than was available in the hackathon. Nevertheless, a fully developed version of the virtual museum could incorporate these accessibility standards to ensure that everyone can use it. To achieve this, the museum and its interactive resources would need to be navigable and operable using a keyboard, rather than relying solely on a mouse. Text content would need to be compatible with screen readers, and images would require alternative texts so that screen readers can communicate their content to users with visual impairments. Furthermore, information would need to be available in both audio and text formats, with captions, transcripts, and alternative text provided when appropriate.

We could also add translations into different languages to allow people who don’t understand English to access the content.

Adding user-paced versions of the stories can also contribute to improving access to the content for certain users.

Do you want to focus on specific missions and pieces of equipment, or tell a broader story about NASA’s exploration?

For the prototype being presented in this edition of the NASA Spaceapps Challenge, several artifacts have been carefully selected to represent different categories:

  • Landers
  • Probes
  • Rovers

The virtual museum includes artifacts that remain in remote locations throughout the solar system and are no longer operational or they are in a non-return trajectory into space. Artifacts that have been destroyed have been excluded because our goal is to simulate the experience of visiting them on their destinations.

Nevertheless, the website has the potential to expand and eventually feature all the artifacts that have contributed to humanity’s understanding  of our solar system, whether abandoned, destroyed, or still operational, ensuring that their contributions are not forgotten. At the bottom of each page, we included a list of potential artifacts that could be included in the near future.

What perspective(s) do you want to highlight?

We would like to highlight the approach we have chosen to introduce the general public to the artifacts that have contributed to humanity’s understanding of the solar system. Our museum offers an interactive experience featuring dialogues that encourage user participation and first-person narratives told from the artifacts' own perspectives. Rather than focusing on the fact that these artifacts have been abandoned in remote locations, we aim to celebrate their achievements and explore how they overcame the many challenges posed by space exploration.

We use a variety of storytelling techniques to keep the experience engaging and avoid repetition. For example, during the visit to the Viking spacecraft or the Surveyor 3 lander, users can participate in simulated conversations with the mission’s artifacts. In the cases of Shoemaker or Pioneer, we present an animation that tells its story, from launch to landing, in the first case, or continuing in the second. For Sojourner, we have included a trivia-style game and the end of its story. In this way, each experience offers something different, helping to maintain visitors’ interest throughout their exploration of the museum.

We would also like to highlight the different ways in which we have made use of NASA’s resources to develop this project. First, we have relied on NASA's documentation and scientific information to research the artifacts and ensure the accuracy of the content we share.

We have also incorporated 3D models of the artifacts obtained from NASA’s resources, along with a tool that allows users to visualize the real time positions of probes travelling through deep space.

Additionally, we have used photographs from NASA’s image archives to create realistic backgrounds for our animations. For instance, Viking Landers 1 and 2 are depicted against backgrounds corresponding to their actual landing sites. The photographs downloaded from NASA’s website were slightly modified using artificial intelligence to adjust the viewing angle and provide a wider view of the sky, allowing the corresponding orbiters to appear in the animations. Despite these modifications, the original landing sites remain clearly recognizable.

Similarly, we used NASA imagery as reference material for AI-generated sprites featured in our interactive stories, helping us create realistic visual representations of the spacecraft. 

How could we spread the news about the museum?

We can use social media, ask NASA to add the link to their website, and spread the news among schools via their authorities.

How could we keep the site up to date?

As NASA declares newer missions finished, we could create new stories to include those new artifacts in our collection.

Intended impact:

NASA provides information on its website about the abandoned (but not forgotten) artifacts that served this goal, but in a format that is not necessarily accessible or engaging for the general public. We aim to encourage new generations to get into science, engage in space exploration, and value the knowledge that all of these missions provided.
